tin8-ban-mau-trinh-chieu.reading: Read part 1 (textbook pages 51–52). In grade 7 you used themes. A theme is a set of colours, fonts and picture effects that gives a presentation one professional look. Presentation software also has templates. A template is a design of one or more slides saved as a .potx file. It has the layout, colours, fonts, effects, background and even content. You can use ready-made templates or make your own, save them, use them again and share them. A template is usually made for one purpose or topic (a trip, a business project, a lesson,…), so its suggested content is also useful. Figure 11a.2 is a travel template: the slides are designed and the topics are suggested.

bm.label: Reading – Templates and themes
bm.q: Do both themes and templates have each part, or only templates?
bm.k: A theme is a set of colours, fonts and picture effects. A template also has the layout, background and suggested content for a topic.
items: Instructions on how to type and present the content

ext.label: Reading – Template files
ext.q: A template is saved as a file with the extension:
ext.k: A template is saved as a .potx file (a normal presentation is .pptx).

p22.label: Question p.22
p22.q: If you copy the formula in cell E4 (=C4*D4) to cells E6, E7, E8 and E9, what are the formulas in those cells?
p22.k: E6: =C6*D6; E7: =C7*D7; E8: =C8*D8; E9: =C9*D9. Relative addresses change with the position of the cell.

tin8-bieu-dien-du-lieu.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 76–77). In Figure 13.1, “Tin học” is text data and 3.141592 is number data. In Figure 13.3, cell C1 adds 3 and 5 and gives the number 8; cell C2 joins the characters 3 and 5 and gives the string 35; cell C3 checks if 3 is less than 5 and gives TRUE, a logical value.
Programming languages sort data into types, so they can store them and use the right operations. Numbers are integers or real numbers; text is characters or strings; conditions and comparisons are logical. Each data type has a set of values and some operations. Scratch has three data types: number, string and Boolean (logical). Each operation gives a value of a certain type.

kieu.label: Reading – Three data types in Scratch
kieu.q: Which Scratch data type is each value?
kieu.k: Number: whole numbers, decimals (15, 3.141592). String: characters or strings (@, Computer, the result of join). Boolean: true or false (the result of a comparison).
items: The result of joining 3 and 5 (35 in cell C2)

pt.label: Reading – Operations (Table 13.2)
pt.q: Match each operation with its result (try it in the simulation).
pt.k: 13 mod 4 = 1; join → “applebanana”; 70 > 50 → true; and is true only when both are true → false; or is false only when both are false → true; not (true) → false.

tin8-bieu-do.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 32–33). Charts show data visually, so it is easy to compare data or see if it goes up or down. Each type of chart has its own use:
  • Column charts are used to compare data.
  • Line charts show how data goes up or down over time (Figure 7.3).
  • Pie charts compare the parts with the whole (Figure 7.4).
Try the chart simulation: choose a data table and a chart type, and see which type fits.

loai.label: Reading – Choose a chart type
loai.q: Read part 1 (textbook pages 32–33). Which chart type should you use in each situation?
loai.k: 1 – a, 2 – b, 3 – c, 4 – b, 5 – a. Column: compare data; line: trend over time; pie: parts of a whole.
items: 1) Compare the number of students interested in each ICT topic
2) See the trend in the number of downloaded apps from 2017 to 2020
3) The percentage of students for each topic out of all students surveyed
4) The average temperature of a city over 12 months
5) Compare the average ICT marks of 5 classes

it.label: Reading – Reading a chart
it.q: In the column chart in Figure 7.2, which ICT topic has the fewest interested students?
it.k: The lowest column is Word processing (2 students). The highest is Computer graphics (15), then Programming languages (8).

tin8-cau-truc-dieu-khien.reading: Read part 1c (textbook page 82). In the game, the player does not guess only once. The player guesses again and again until the secret number is found. Each time the guess is wrong, the computer asks again and compares the new answer with the secret number. The loop repeats only when the guess is wrong, so a correct guess is the stop condition of the loop. Figure 14.4a shows the algorithm, and Scratch uses the block “repeat until” (Figure 14.4d). Scratch has three loop blocks: repeat a fixed number of times (Figure 14.4b), forever (Figure 14.4c) and repeat until a condition (Figure 14.4d).

ct.label: Reading – Three control structures
ct.q: Which control structure does each block or description show?
ct.k: Sequence: blocks joined in order. Branching: if … then (one branch), if … then … else (two branches). Loop: repeat n, forever, repeat until.
items: Joining blocks in order from top to bottom

lap.label: Reading – Three kinds of loops
lap.q: Match each Scratch loop block with its kind of loop (Figure 14.4).
lap.k: repeat 10 – a; forever – b; repeat until – c (stops when the condition is true).
opts: a) Repeat a fixed number of times
c) Repeat until a condition is true

tin8-danh-sach-hinh-anh.reading: Read part 1 (textbook page 37). Word processors have two kinds of lists: bulleted lists and numbered lists. The survey in Figure 8a.1 is a numbered list. Figure 8a.3 has a numbered list with a bulleted list inside. Each item in a list is a paragraph; you press Enter to start a new item. In a bulleted list, each item starts with a bullet. In a numbered list, each item starts with a number or a letter and a full stop or a bracket. Bullets and numbers are added and updated automatically when you add or delete items. Lists make a document clear and nice, and help readers find information quickly. Try it in the simulation below.

kieu.label: Reading – Choose a kind of list
kieu.q: Read part 1 (textbook pages 36–37). Which content needs a numbered list, and which only needs a bulleted list?
kieu.k: When the order matters (steps, rankings), use a numbered list. When the items are equal, use a bulleted list.
items: The steps to shut down a computer safely
The steps to cook rice in a rice cooker
Things to bring on a picnic
The top three teams in a football league

tin8-dao-duc-van-hoa-so.reading: Read part 1 (textbook pages 18–19). Digital technology brings many benefits but also problems: rude, unethical or even illegal behaviour of people who use or create digital content. Examples: filming in a cinema; taking photos where it is not allowed (Figure 4.1); recording conversations without permission; downloading copyrighted songs or videos without permission; copying information from a website and saying it is yours; using cracked software; livestreaming or sharing school violence; posting other people's personal information without permission; joining, sharing or advertising websites about violence or gambling,… You need to learn about the law (Figure 4.2).

bh.label: Reading – A violation or not?
bh.q: Read part 1 (textbook pages 18–19). Is each action unethical, illegal or rude?
bh.k: The first four actions are violations. Listening to music on a licensed app, and using a photo with permission and the author's name, are right.
items: Taking photos where there is a no-photo sign (Figure 4.1)
Listening to music on a licensed app
Using a friend's photo with permission and with the author's name

tin8-dau-trang-chan-trang.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 42–43). The Header and the Footer are the top part (top margin) and the bottom part (bottom margin) of a document. They are separate from the main text (Figure 9a.3) and often have notes, page numbers, the document title, the author's name,… They can also have pictures. Information in the header and footer appears on every page automatically, so you can keep some information through the whole document. It also makes the pages look professional. Example: in Figure 9a.2 the header and footer show the title “Project document”, page number “1” and “ICT Club”.
Try it in the simulation: click Header ▾ → Blank and type a line — it appears on both pages.

vitri.label: Reading – Where does it go?
vitri.q: Does each piece of information usually go in the header/footer or in the main text?
vitri.k: The header and footer have short information repeated on every page: page number, title, author, notes, logo. The main content goes in the main text.

tin8-go-loi.tag: Reading a) Testing · b) Kinds of errors
tin8-go-loi.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 86–87). The game should show the number of guesses when the player finds the secret number. But when you run it, the number shown is always one less than the real number of guesses. Running a program to check it is called testing. Testing finds unusual situations, called errors (bugs). We must remove errors before the program is finished and shared.
The program still runs, but it does not follow the plan. There are two kinds of errors: 1) a syntax error happens when a command breaks the rules of the programming language, so the program does not run; 2) a logic error happens when the commands are written correctly but the program does not do what the plan says, like in the Guess the Number game.

loai.label: Reading – Two kinds of errors
loai.q: Is each error a syntax error or a logic error?
loai.k: Syntax error: breaks the rules, the program does not run. Logic error: correct syntax but the program does the wrong thing.
items: A command breaks the rules of the language, so the program does not run
Typing the wrong command name (prnt instead of print) in a text-based language
The number of guesses shown is one less than the real number
Using “+” instead of “join” to join text and numbers
The game allows more than 7 guesses but the plan says only 7

tin8-khai-thac-thong-tin-so.reading:
Step 3. Decide the level and the requirements of the presentation. For example:

tin8-luoc-su-cong-cu-tinh-toan.reading:
With new technology, electronic computers can be divided into five generations:
  • 1st generation (1945 – 1955): vacuum tubes; magnetic drum memory; very big. Example: ENIAC (Figure 1.4).
  • 2nd generation (1955 – 1965): transistors; magnetic core and magnetic tape memory. Examples: IBM 7090, Minsk-22 (came to Viet Nam in 1968).
  • 3rd generation (1965 – 1974): integrated circuits (IC). Example: IBM System/360 (came to Viet Nam in 1967).
  • 4th generation (1974 – 1990): very large scale integration (VLSI) and microprocessors; CD, RAM, ROM, USB, SSD. Examples: Micral, IBM PC, Apple II.
  • 5th generation (1990 – today): ultra large scale integration (ULSI), parallel processing, artificial intelligence. Examples: smartphones, smart speakers, smart glasses.

the.label: Reading – Five generations
the.q: Read part 2 (textbook pages 7–8). Match each generation with its main electronic part.
the.k: 1 – a, 2 – b, 3 – c, 4 – d, 5 – e. Each generation made electronic parts smaller, so devices became smaller, faster and used less energy.
opts: d) Very large scale integration (VLSI) and microprocessors

bm.label: Reading – Memory
bm.q: Was each kind of memory used mainly in old computers (1st, 2nd generation) or new computers (4th generation and later)?
bm.k: 1st generation: magnetic drum; 2nd: magnetic core, magnetic tape; 4th: CD, RAM, ROM, USB, SSD,…

tin8-sap-xep-va-loc-du-lieu.reading: Read part 1 (textbook pages 27–28). Each survey answer is one row in the spreadsheet; each name is split into Middle name and First name. The survey helps decide how to run the ICT Club, for example: (1) Sort the names in alphabetical order so they are easy to find; (2) Which students want to learn each ICT topic? (3) Which topic do most students choose? (4) Which groups are the students in, to make study groups? Use the simulation below to try sorting and filtering.

cn.label: Reading – Sort or filter?
cn.q: Read part 1 (textbook pages 27–28). Should you sort or filter the data for each request?
cn.k: Sort: change the order of the rows by one or more criteria. Filter: show only the rows that meet a condition; the other rows are hidden.

Show only the classes with no students using digital devices for 5 hours or more

nd.label: Reading – The most popular
nd.q: In the survey results of class 8A (Figure 6.2), which ICT topic do most students choose?
nd.k: Programming languages – 4 students: Vũ Thị Minh An, Trần Minh Châu, Đặng Mai Trang, Phùng Khánh Toàn. You can filter the Topic column to get this list.

tin8-thong-tin-trong-moi-truong-so.reading:
Read part 2 (textbook pages 12–13). Unreliable information can be dishonest and misleading; rumours that lead to conclusions without evidence; or unchecked information that leads to wrong decisions. Tips to find reliable information:
  • Check the source: who gives the information and how trusted they are (a blog is less reliable because anyone can write a blog).
  • Tell opinions from facts: an opinion is a point of view and is less reliable than a fact.
  • Check the evidence: a conclusion without evidence is very unreliable.
  • Check how recent it is: a web page that is not updated for a long time is usually less reliable.

cach.label: Reading – How to check
cach.q: Read part 2 (textbook pages 12–13). Which tip does each action follow?
items: 1) Check if the news is in an official newspaper or on a personal blog
2) Notice that “I think this is the best film” is only a personal view
3) Look for numbers and evidence for the conclusion
4) Check when the web page was last updated
opts: d) Check how recent it is

ys.label: Reading – Opinion or fact?
ys.q: Is each sentence an opinion (a personal view) or a fact (it happened and can be checked)?
ys.k: An opinion is a point of view, often with feelings and bias, so it is less reliable than a fact. A fact happened and can be checked.
items: “I think this is the best cartoon of all time.”
In 1642, Blaise Pascal built the mechanical calculator Pascaline.
“This dish is surely the best in the city.”
The Vietnamese team won 2–0 last night.

tin8-tin-hoc-nghe-nghiep.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 91–92). In history, technology has always changed how workers in every job do their work. Today ICT is used in almost every job and makes work more effective because:
  • It speeds up processing and saves time. Example: accountants use software to do in minutes what took hours by hand; payments and transfers happen almost at once online.
  • It makes communication easy. Documents and messages reach colleagues and customers around the world at once.
  • It supports teamwork and wider work. Example: programmers work across borders with online tools, hold online meetings and edit the same document in the cloud.
  • It helps improve skills and gives information. Example: taxi drivers use booking apps, maps and traffic alerts to find customers and avoid traffic jams.

li.label: Reading – ICT makes work more effective
li.q: Which benefit of ICT does each example show?
li.k: Four benefits: faster processing; easy communication; teamwork and wider work; better skills and information.
items: Accountants calculate with software in minutes; payments are almost instant
Documents and messages reach colleagues and customers around the world at once
Programmers work across borders on one shared document in the cloud
Taxi drivers use booking apps, maps and traffic alerts to find the way

nghe.label: Reading – ICT jobs and related jobs
nghe.q: Is each job an ICT job or a job that uses ICT?
nghe.k: ICT jobs: software developer, mobile app programmer, network administrator, web developer and designer. Jobs that use ICT: online seller, streamer, vlogger.

h161.label: Reading – Figure 16.1
h161.q: Match each ICT application with the job in Figure 16.1.
h161.k: Doctor – health records, remote check-ups; Journalist – online newspaper; Tourism manager – booking website; Office worker – word processing, storing files; Architect – design, 3D printing; Agricultural engineer – automatic watering, IoT.
items: Posting articles quickly in an online newspaper

tin8-trang-chieu-nang-cao.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 46–47). Text on slides is different from text in a document: it is short and shows only the main ideas. Good slide text impresses the audience and helps them understand quickly. Colours are also very important: a nice, professional presentation combines content, layout and colour. Some tips:
  • Warm colours (red, orange, yellow,…) feel warm and make people lively and active.
  • Cool colours (blue, purple,…) feel cool and make people calm and gentle.
  • Neutral colours (white, black, beige,…) feel polite and soft.
  • The main colours should match the content: entertainment and festivals → warm colours; education → neutral colours; art, strong impressions, thank-you events → cool colours.
  • Combine colours from the same group (red, orange, yellow with brown; blue, green with grey).
  • Do not use too many colours on one slide.
  • Choose a text colour with high contrast to the background.

mau.label: Reading – Colour groups
mau.q: Put each colour in the right group.
mau.k: Warm (warm, lively, active): red, orange, yellow. Cool (calm, gentle): blue, purple, green. Neutral (polite, soft): white, black, beige.

gam.label: Reading – Colours for each topic
gam.q: Which colour group should each presentation use?
gam.k: Entertainment, festivals → warm. Education → neutral. Art, strong impressions, thank-you events → cool.

nt.label: Reading – Tips for choosing colours
nt.q: Is each idea a do or a don't?
nt.k: Do: combine colours from the same group; text with high contrast to the background; main colours that match the content. Don't: use too many colours; text and background in the same tone (hard to read).
items: Combine colours from the same group (red, orange, yellow with brown)
Use lots of colours on one slide to stand out
Choose a text colour with high contrast to the background
Yellow text on a light yellow background
Choose main colours that match the content

tin8-tu-thuat-toan-den-chuong-trinh.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 73–74). An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles of 60 degrees. To move along an equilateral triangle, the sprite repeats two actions three times: move forward a number of steps equal to the side (for example 60 steps); turn left 120 degrees. The algorithm uses a sequence and a loop that repeats 3 times (the number of sides). After three times the loop stops. Figure 12.3a shows the flowchart.
Besides words and flowcharts, we can write a program so the computer “understands” and runs the algorithm. The Scratch program in Figure 12.3b does each step of the flowchart with a Scratch command. So a program is a sequence of commands that makes the computer carry out an algorithm.

map.label: Reading – From flowchart to program
map.q: Match each part of the flowchart (Figure 12.3a) with the Scratch command (Figure 12.3b).
map.k: Start – a; the three loop control boxes – b (repeat 3); Move 60 steps – c; Turn left 120 degrees – d (turn ↺ 120 degrees).

ct.label: Reading – Programs
ct.k: A program is a sequence of commands that makes the computer carry out an algorithm.
o: A sequence of commands that makes the computer carry out an algorithm.
A flowchart that describes an algorithm.
A drawing on the Scratch stage.
